subcategory: cool-season cottage annual with orchid-like blooms

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, barely covering the fine seed, and transplant out once nights stay above freezing.

directions: Sow seed indoors on the surface of moist starting mix and keep in a cool, bright spot, since seedlings resent heat and stretch badly if grown too warm. Pinch young plants once or twice to encourage bushy branching, then move outdoors after hardening off to a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates. The finely divided, fern-like foliage is topped with masses of small, intricately patterned flowers in pink, magenta, purple, and white that resemble miniature orchids, making it a favorite for cool greenhouse displays, container plantings, and shaded borders where summers are mild.

subcategory: compact tender bedding and container annual

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost since it is slow to reach blooming size, and transplant outdoors only once nights are reliably warm.

directions: Press the tiny seed onto the surface of a moist, well-draining seed mix and keep warm and humid under cover, as it germinates slowly and needs light to sprout. Grow on in bright, indirect light and pinch seedlings once to build a rounded mound before setting plants out in a sheltered spot with dappled shade in hot regions. Compact plants form neat domes of glossy foliage covered in small, fragrant, saucer-shaped violet-blue or white flowers with contrasting yellow anthers, making it a long-blooming choice for shaded borders, window boxes, and indoor pots.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

subcategory: papery everlasting for drying and cutting

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost, or as soon as the ground can be worked, since this fine-rooted annual dislikes transplanting.

directions: Scatter seed thinly over well-drained soil and press in lightly, then thin seedlings once they have true leaves because crowded plants stretch and flop. Provide lean, gritty soil and steady sun, as overly rich conditions produce weak stems and fewer blooms. Wiry stems carry papery, daisy-form flowers in pink, rose, and white with a bright central disc that keep their color and shape when air dried, making this a classic everlasting for dried arrangements as well as a cheerful cut flower fresh from the garden.

subcategory: small-flowered everlasting for edging and drying

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date once soil has warmed slightly, or start indoors a few weeks earlier where the growing season is short.

directions: Sow shallowly in well-drained soil after frost danger passes and keep evenly moist until seedlings establish, then let the planting dry down slightly between waterings once mature. Compact, finely branched plants form tidy mounds of ferny foliage topped with dense, flat clusters of tiny golden-yellow everlasting flowers that resemble a sunny take on ageratum. The long-lasting blooms hold their color well after cutting and drying, making this an easy, low-maintenance edging plant and a useful filler for dried bouquets.

planting.note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks earlier for an earlier display.

directions: Sow directly in well-drained soil once nights stay warm, since this Mediterranean native thrives in heat and resents soggy conditions. Space plants generously to let their rounded, bushy habit fill out, and pinch young growth to encourage more branching and flowers. Bright green, aromatic, feathery foliage is covered from midsummer into fall with cheerful yellow daisy blooms that open from lime-green buds, giving borders and gravel gardens a long season of drought-tolerant color and making it a useful filler for late-summer cutting gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost danger has passed, since this fast-growing heat lover resents cool, wet conditions.

directions: Scatter seed over warm, well-drained soil and rake in lightly, thinning seedlings to give the spreading stems room to sprawl. Once established, plants tolerate heat, humidity, and dry spells with little fuss, blooming steadily from early summer until frost. Low, trailing stems are studded with small, single, zinnia-like flowers in gold or orange with dark purple-black centers, making it an excellent groundcover, hanging basket filler, or edging plant for hot Southern gardens where many other annuals falter.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date in well-drained soil, or start indoors a few weeks earlier where summers are short.

directions: Sow shallowly in lean, fast-draining soil, since rich or waterlogged ground leads to soft growth and fewer flowers. Once seedlings are established, water only moderately, as this coastal native prefers to dry out between waterings and holds up well to salt spray and heat. Low, trailing plants form a dense mat of succulent foliage smothered in funnel-shaped blue flowers with white and yellow throats that resemble small morning glories, opening fresh each day through summer and making a striking edging, groundcover, or spiller for containers and hanging baskets.

subcategory: wild-type cool-season larkspur for meadows and cutting

planting.note: Direct sow in fall a few weeks before the first hard frost, or as early as possible in spring, since seed needs a cool spell to germinate well.

directions: Scatter seed directly where plants are to grow, since larkspur taproots resist transplanting, and lightly rake it into loosened soil in fall or very early spring while the ground is still cool. Thin crowded seedlings once they emerge and let plants overwinter as small rosettes where hardy. Slender, branching stems carry loose spikes of small, spurred blue-violet flowers over finely cut, airy foliage, giving a wilder, more open look than the taller cultivated larkspurs and providing an easy self-seeding source of early cut flowers and pollinator forage for meadow-style plantings.

subcategory: seed-pod cut flower and dried arrangement annual

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring while the soil is still cool, since this species resents root disturbance and grows best from an undisturbed sowing.

directions: Sow seed directly in well-drained soil as soon as it can be worked and keep evenly moist until germination, then let plantings dry down somewhat once established. Unlike the frilly-petaled love-in-a-mist grown for its flowers, this species is prized for its unusual seed capsules, small yellow-green flowers with feathery bracts give way to star-shaped, spiky green pods that mature to tan and hold their odd form when dried. The airy foliage and architectural pods make it a favorite for fresh and dried cut-flower arrangements rather than for garden color alone.

subcategory: fragrant cool-season candytuft for cutting and edging

planting.note: Direct sow a few weeks before the last frost in cool soil, since this hardy annual germinates and grows best in cooler temperatures.

directions: Sow seed shallowly in well-drained soil as soon as it can be worked, then thin seedlings to their final spacing since crowded plants produce fewer flower spikes. Succession sow every few weeks in spring for a continuous supply of blooms before summer heat shortens the display. Unlike the flat-topped clusters of common candytuft, this species bears dense, upright, hyacinth-like spikes of small, fragrant white or lilac flowers that are excellent for cutting and draw bees and other pollinators to the border or cutting garden.
